strengths: Addresses a practically important problem: annotation-free 6D pose estimation and tracking from a single 3D model, with an automatic re-registration mechanism that could reduce deployment overhead in robotics and manufacturing.

The SOM segmentation results are promising on several BOP datasets: mean mAP 68.5, above the supervised ZebraPose baseline (67.5) and unsupervised baselines, with relatively fast inference (0.183 s/image) and strong gains on LM-O, HomebrewedDB, and YCB-Video.
The tracking module TOM shows a clear improvement over FoundationPose tracking on the modified YCB-Video setup (ADD 74.64 vs 52.76, AR 67.85 vs 50.09) with modest reported overhead.

The attention-based tracking-failure classifier is ablated against cosine similarity and no-attention variants, reaching 98.36% accuracy in Table 4, and the paper includes additional ablations on language injection, HSFA depth, and DINOv2 fine-tuning.

The system design is a reasonable engineering integration of vision-language prompting, DINOv2 features, SAM2/FastSAM, and FoundationPose, and the attempt to open-source the custom tracking dataset is useful.
weaknesses: The central 'annotation-free'/'self-supervised' claim is not convincingly supported. The segmentation loss in Eq. (2) uses pixel-level ground-truth labels t_i, and Appendix D describes augmenting 'each query image and its corresponding mask'. If these masks come from BOP training annotations, then SOM is trained with human-annotated segmentation masks, contradicting the abstract's claim of requiring no manual annotation and invalidating the 'self-supervised' comparison in Table 2.

Reproducibility is weakened by multiple inconsistencies: the code link is missing; TOM is trained for 15 epochs in the main text but 10 epochs in Appendix D; the hardware is described as eight A100 GPUs for SOM in one place and an RTX A6000 in another; the loss hyperparameters in the main text (α=0.3, β=0.7, λ_T=1.0, λ_f=0.2) conflict with Appendix D (Focal weight 20, Tversky weight 0.2, α=0.5, β=0.5, plus Dice/IoU losses not in the main text). The HSFA algorithm also differs from the text description regarding when raw versus refined reference features are used in cross-attention.

The pose-estimation evaluation is too limited for the state-of-the-art claim. Table 1 compares only FoundationPose+CNOS and FoundationPose+ground-truth masks on LM-O and YCB-Video, with no comparisons to other annotation-free or supervised 6D pose methods and no results on the other BOP datasets used for segmentation. The claim of 'state-of-the-art accuracy on challenging industrial datasets' is therefore not substantiated.

There is a factual error in the segmentation results: the text claims SOM 'establishes a new state-of-the-art on four out of the five benchmarks—LM-O, T-LESS, HomebrewedDB, and YCB-Video', but Table 2 shows SOM is best only on LM-O, HomebrewedDB, and YCB-Video; on T-LESS it is 47.1 versus ZebraPose's 72.1, and on TUD-L it is 69.1 versus ZebraPose's 71.8. This overclaim undermines confidence in the reported comparisons.

The tracking evaluation does not isolate the value of failure detection. Table 3 reports final pose recall on modified YCB-Video but not detection precision/recall, false-positive rate, recovery success rate, or threshold sensitivity. The improvement could come from more frequent re-registration rather than the classifier, and no oracle-failure or periodic re-registration baseline is provided.

The custom tracking-failure dataset is synthetic and may not reflect real tracking failures. Negative samples are generated from different objects or random crops, which can make the binary classification task easier than real drift/occlusion detection; there is no validation of the classifier on a separate real-world tracking-failure benchmark.

The methodological novelty is incremental: the pipeline largely composes off-the-shelf components (DINOv2, CLIP, an LLM, SAM2/FastSAM, FoundationPose), while HSFA and AdaNorm-based text injection are standard attention/FiLM-style mechanisms. The tracking module is a lightweight binary classifier over concatenated DINOv2 features. The paper does not provide a theoretical or algorithmic advance beyond system integration.

The 'real-time' claim is questionable: TOM reports 98 ms and SOM reports 183 ms, so when re-registration is triggered the full pipeline can exceed 280 ms per frame (~3.5 FPS), which is not real-time for many robotics applications. End-to-end latency with re-registration frequency is not reported.

The paper lacks a limitations discussion and failure analysis. It does not analyze sensitivity to LLM/CLIP description errors, textureless or symmetric objects, 3D model quality, severe occlusion, or dataset licensing/bias. This is especially important given the strong annotation-free and robustness claims.

Some citations and references are inconsistent or unclear, e.g., SAM-6D is cited as Lin et al. 2024 but the reference key is Lin et al. 2017, and CNOS is cited as Nguyen et al. 2023 but keyed as Nguyen et al. 2019. Several baselines are taken from the BOP leaderboard without peer-reviewed references, making fair comparison difficult.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely important and practical problem: annotation-free 6D pose estimation and tracking with explicit recovery from tracking failures, which is a real weakness in render-and-refine trackers like FoundationPose.

The overall pipeline (multi-view rendering -> semantic prompting -> HSFA feature fusion -> foundation segmentation -> pose -> tracking-loss classifier -> re-registration) is a coherent and plausible engineering combination, and the idea of reformulating tracking-loss detection as a lightweight classification task is sensible and efficient.
Includes some ablation studies (HSFA layer count, language injection, DINOv2 fine-tuning, attention vs. cosine similarity for tracking loss), which is a step toward justifying design choices.
Reports real-time-ish runtimes and claims open-source code, which if accurate would aid reproducibility and deployment.
weaknesses: The headline results are implausible and unsupported. In Table 2 the 'self-supervised' SOM reaches 68.5 mean mAP, surpassing the supervised ZebraPose (67.5) and beating the best unsupervised method (NOCTIS, 56.8) by ~12 points, including 89.3 on YCB-V vs 73.1 for the supervised baseline. No explanation is offered for why a method requiring no per-object training would so dramatically outperform supervised baselines, and the supervision-level categorization ('self-supervised' for STORM vs. 'unsupervised' for CNOS/SAM6D) is not defined or justified.

The central claim that STORM is 'annotation-free/label-free' is contradicted by the method itself. Appendix F states TOM training uses ground-truth masks from BOP, and Appendix D's augmentation pipeline operates on masks during SOM training. The paper never clarifies the provenance of these masks, directly undermining the annotation-free framing used throughout the abstract and contributions.

The abstract/introduction claim 'without additional training,' yet SOM is trained for ~80,000 steps on 8 A100s and TOM for 10-15 epochs. This is misleading; the real claim (no per-instance retraining) is not what is written.

Hyperparameters and training details are mutually inconsistent between the main text and appendix, which severely harms reproducibility. Examples: main text gives Tversky α=0.3, β=0.7 and focal weight λ_f=0.2 (Eq. 2), while Appendix D gives Tversky α=β=0.5 and focal weight 20.0; main text says '15 epochs' for TOM, appendix says 10; main text says AdamW for both modules, appendix says SGD for SOM and Adam for TOM. The appendix also introduces Dice and IoU losses never mentioned in the main text.

The pose-estimation evaluation (Table 1) is weak and the claims drawn from it are unsupported. STORM is reported to exactly match the ground-truth-mask FoundationPose baseline on YCB-V (0.78/0.99/0.74) and to be within 4% on LM-O, leading to the claim of pose estimates 'nearly indistinguishable' from manual annotations. Given SOM is a learned segmenter, matching GT masks exactly is extraordinary and unexplained; ADD/ADD-S values are reported as unitless fractions without clarity on normalization, and no statistical variability or per-object breakdown is provided.

The tracking evaluation (Table 3) uses an artificial protocol that favors the proposed method: YCB-V is modified by randomly dropping frames and masking object regions to induce failures, which is precisely the regime where the baseline has no recovery mechanism. No comparison is made to other failure-detection or re-detection strategies, so the reported 74.64 vs 52.76 ADD gap does not establish general superiority.

Baseline coverage is thin. For pose estimation only CNOS+FP and FP+GT are compared; no comparison against other CAD-based segmentation methods integrated with FP, and the 'DINO-based pipeline' mentioned in the setup never appears in any results table. For tracking, no comparison to DeepIM/RBPF/6-PACK-style recovery or SiamR-CNN-style re-detection.

Novelty is incremental and over-claimed. HSFA is essentially cross/self-attention between query and rendered reference features with AdaNorm-based text injection, closely related to prior reference-based segmentation work; the tracking-loss classifier is a single self-attention + linear head; the memory-pool re-registration is standard. None of these is positioned against the specific prior mechanisms they purport to improve.

Presentation and scholarship problems: Figure 1 is described with contradictory captions ('camera pose variation' vs 'camera rotation'); the reference list contains multiple errors (Sam-6D attributed to Lin et al. 2017, duplicate 'Lin et al. 2017' keys, He et al. 2020/2021 mislabeled years); several tables have inconsistent formatting and units; numerous grammatical errors throughout. These make the technical content harder to verify.

Reproducibility is insufficient: the 'in-house' tracking dataset is only sketched (100k positive / 100k negative pairs) with no link or detailed spec; the exact training-set composition and its overlap with the BOP test sets is ambiguous; and key components (exact SOM loss in the main text, AdaNorm-Zero details, re-registration threshold) are underspecified.
No ablation links segmentation quality to downstream pose accuracy, so the reader cannot assess how errors in SOM propagate to 6D pose or how sensitive the system is to the tracking-loss threshold.

strengths: STORM addresses a practical and important problem: annotation-free 6D pose estimation and tracking from only a single 3D model, reducing deployment overhead for robotics and industrial vision.

The SOM segmentation results are strong: Table 2 reports a mean mAP of 68.5 on five BOP datasets with 0.183 s inference time, outperforming the mean of supervised baselines and many unsupervised methods.

The HSFA ablation is convincing: Table 6 shows that 0-layer HSFA collapses to 44.0 AP while 3-layer HSFA reaches 94.6 AP, indicating that the proposed hierarchical attention fusion is a critical component.
The tracking-loss classifier is lightweight and effective on the authors' dataset: Table 4 shows 98.36% accuracy with 1 attention layer and only 1.3 ms additional latency over cosine similarity.

The TOM tracking experiments on modified YCB-Video show large gains over FoundationPose tracking (Table 3: ADD 74.64 vs 52.76, AR 67.85 vs 50.09), and Figure 4 provides a qualitative recovery example.
The appendix includes training details, hyperparameters, and ablation studies, showing an effort toward transparency and reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central SOTA claim is contradicted by the paper's own table: Table 2 shows STORM is second-best on T-LESS (47.1 vs ZebraPose 72.1) and TUD-L (69.1 vs 71.8), yet the text claims new SOTA on four of five benchmarks. This undermines the main conclusion.

Training data is ambiguous and may involve benchmark leakage: Appendix C says SOM is trained on LMO, LM, YCBV, HB, TLESS, TUDL, TYOL, and RU-APC. Since LMO, YCBV, HB, TLESS, and TUDL are evaluation datasets, it is unclear whether test images or only training splits were used. If target test data were used for training, the zero-shot/annotation-free claim is weakened.
The abstract claim 'without additional training' is false: SOM and TOM are both trained on large datasets. The system is annotation-free in terms of masks, but not training-free.

The 'real-time' claim is not supported end-to-end: SOM takes 0.183 s per image, TOM adds 98 ms, and FoundationPose pose estimation/inference is not included in the timing. The full pipeline is likely well below typical real-time control rates.

Pose estimation evaluation is limited: Table 1 only compares against FoundationPose+CNOS and FoundationPose+GT masks. There is no comparison to other annotation-free pose methods, and the pose estimator itself is FoundationPose, so the contribution is mainly segmentation rather than pose estimation.

Tracking evaluation is limited: Table 3 only compares against FoundationPose tracking on synthetically modified YCB-Video (dropped frames, random masks). There is no comparison to other trackers, no real-world occlusion benchmark, and no analysis of false positive/negative tracking-loss detection.

The exact equality between STORM and FoundationPose+GT on YCB-Video for all three metrics (ADD 0.78, ADD-S 0.99, AR 0.74) is suspicious and needs explanation; it may indicate metric saturation, rounding, or an evaluation issue.

Reproducibility is weak: the manuscript says 'Code:' but provides no link; the LLM prompt, CLIP/AdaNorm-Zero injection details, HSFA dimensions, exact training splits, and the tracking dataset release are not adequately specified.

Runtime reporting is inconsistent: Table 2 reports 0.183 s for SOM, while Table 5 reports 0.265 s with language and 0.196 s without language. Since the full SOM uses language, the 0.183 s value is unexplained.

Presentation quality is poor: there are numerous citation errors (e.g., SAM-6D attributed to Lin et al. 2017, DINOv2 to Oquab et al. 2015, CNOS to Nguyen et al. 2019, BOP to Hodân et al. 2020), missing or inconsistent table formatting, and no limitations section.
There is no discussion of limitations, failure modes, ethical considerations of LLM/VLM prompting, dependence on 3D model quality, or computational cost of the LLM/CLIP/SAM components.

strengths: Addresses an important and practically relevant problem: annotation-free, reference-conditioned 6D pose tracking with explicit tracking-failure detection.

The system integrates reference-conditioned segmentation (SOM/HSFA) with a learned tracking verifier (TOM) in a coherent closed-loop pipeline, and the temporal energy-like decision rule is a sensible way to avoid brittle per-frame re-initialization.

SOM achieves strong BOP segmentation results in the single-reference, annotation-free setting, with competitive accuracy against both annotation-free and supervised baselines and a favorable runtime profile.

TOM is evaluated on a synthetic failure dataset and a controlled YCB-Video stress test; the attention-based verifier improves failure detection over cosine similarity and a learned baseline, and the temporal policy substantially reduces false re-localizations.
The paper includes a detailed appendix with training details, runtime profiling, threshold calibration, and an honest limitations section that clarifies the scope of the zero-shot claim.
weaknesses: The central annotation-free/no-CAD claim is not convincingly supported. The main pose-estimation results in Table 1 do not specify the object-model source, and the text states that 'only the mask source differs' across methods, implying that ground-truth CAD models may be used for all methods. If so, the pose results do not test the annotation-free claim. Alternatively, if STORM uses SAM3D reconstructions, they are aligned to benchmark CAD models in Appendix G.2, again requiring CAD at evaluation. Without CAD alignment, SAM3D+FP performance is much worse (Table 3), and no deployment experiment with a self-consistent reconstructed object frame is provided.

The abstract and introduction claim robustness under 'severe occlusions and rapid viewpoint changes', but the reported tracking stress test uses only mild perturbations with probability 0.1 (Appendix H.4). The severe setting is not shown, so the claim is overstated relative to the evidence.

Table 2 has a confusing/inconsistent grouping: ZebraPoseSAT and CosyPose are placed under 'Annotation / adaptation-free' even though the text says they are fine-tuned per object category. Baselines lack variance estimates, and STORM's 67.7 mean AP versus ZebraPoseSAT's 67.5 is within reported seed variation, making the 'new state-of-the-art' claim statistically weak.

Pose estimation is compared only against FoundationPose+CNOS and a ground-truth-mask oracle. Recent zero-shot pose methods such as SAM-6D and Pos3R are mentioned but not evaluated in the pose tables. Tracking recovery is compared only against FoundationPose tracking, not against other failure-detection or recovery strategies.

Reproducibility is limited: no code or data release is indicated, the synthetic tracking-failure benchmark is not publicly available, and some architectural details (e.g., exact HSFA block design and TOM attention implementation) are described only at a high level.

Novelty is incremental: the method composes frozen foundation models (DINOv3, CLIP/VLM, SAM3D, FoundationPose) with attention-based segmentation and a binary verifier. The 'energy-like score' is simply the negative compatibility logit, and the paper acknowledges it is not trained with an energy-based objective, so the framing slightly oversells the technical contribution.

Presentation issues include numerous incorrect or inconsistent references (e.g., years and citations), a possible typo/undefined use of 'TOM' early in the introduction, and unclear metric naming (mAP vs AP_C) in the main segmentation table.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely relevant problem (annotation-free, reference-conditioned 6D pose estimation and tracking) and proposes a coherent two-stage pipeline that couples segmentation, geometry, and failure verification.
SOM achieves competitive segmentation numbers on BOP datasets, and the paper reports single-reference performance and latency, which is useful for the practical setting it targets.

The paper provides several ablations (HSFA depth, attention in TOM, reference count, language conditioning) and an honest, detailed Limitations section that explicitly scopes the zero-shot claim to annotation-free/adaptation-free inference rather than category-disjoint generalization.

The TOM verifier with EMA smoothing and an L-consecutive-frame rule is a sensible engineering design, and Appendix H.2 shows the temporal policy substantially reduces transient false re-localizations.
weaknesses: Central claims are overstated relative to the evidence. Table 1 states STORM 'matches the ground-truth setup exactly' on YCB-V, but the values are 77/98/73 vs. 78/99/74, i.e. consistently ~1 point below GT. Similarly, Table 2 claims a 'new state-of-the-art' with AP_C 67.7 vs. ZebraPoseSAT's 67.5 — a 0.2-point difference that is well within STORM's own ±1.44 std and overlaps the baseline; on T-LESS the gap is huge (53.0 vs 72.1). These are not supported as stated.

The geometric-anchoring evidence is circular. In Table 3, 'SAM3D (aligned)' is aligned to the benchmark CAD via ICP (Appendix G.2), so the near-parity with GT+FP is largely a consequence of fitting to the GT model; the unaligned model collapses (VSD 22.19 vs 60.72). This directly undercuts the 'no curated CAD models' narrative, and the aligned ADD-S AUC (99.12) exceeding the GT upper bound (98.95) is unexplained. The claim that reconstructed geometry is 'sufficient' is therefore not established without GT-CAD-based alignment.

The tracking contribution (TOM) is not evaluated on any standard tracking benchmark. Table 4 uses a self-constructed, corrupted YCB-V stress test, and the STORM-vs-FoundationPose comparison confounds TOM with re-initialization (STORM is given a recovery mechanism the baseline lacks), so it does not isolate the verifier's effect. Table 5 is likewise evaluated only on the authors' synthetic failure dataset, with no cross-dataset or cross-domain generalization evidence.

The 'energy-like' framing is superficial. The paper itself concedes that E = -g_theta is only an inference-time transformation of a BCE logit with no energy-based training, so the OOD/energy-detection analogy adds little beyond a learned classifier thresholded over time. This weakens the stated contribution of 'formulating tracking verification' as novel.

Originality is limited. HSFA is described as adapting 'established attention operations' (self-/cross-attention, AdaLN/FiLM conditioning), TOM is a small binary compatibility classifier, and the pipeline leans heavily on frozen DINOv3, CLIP, SAM3D, and FoundationPose. The trainable contribution is an assembly of existing modules, and the paper does not clearly delineate what is genuinely new versus inherited.

Presentation and citation quality are poor. The reference list has numerous year/author mismatches (e.g., Cremers & Kolev cited as 2025 but referenced 2010; Pos3R cited as Deng et al. 2021 but dated 2025; Hinterstoisser 2020 vs 2012). Table 2's layout is garbled (a stray 'Mask R-CNN' header row; CosyPose/Mask R-CNN rows appear duplicated/mislabeled), and the paper leaves a placeholder 'Conflict of Interest Disclosure.' with no content, signaling an unfinished submission.

Comparability and reproducibility concerns: baselines are reported without variance while STORM is reported with 5-seed std, making differences hard to interpret; there is no statement of code/model release; and the pipeline depends on many frozen foundation models plus 8×A100 training, which will hinder independent reproduction.

Several quantitative comparisons lack controls: Table 1 compares a single STORM run against a single baseline point estimate; the '5% improvement' framing on YCB-V rests on unpaired numbers; and the head-to-head with supervised baselines mixes protocols (runtime from a leaderboard vs. H100 measurement), so the efficiency and SOTA claims are not cleanly established.

strengths: The paper presents a unified, annotation-free pipeline for reference-conditioned 6D pose tracking that combines segmentation, geometry, and tracking-failure detection, reducing reliance on CAD models or manual masks at inference.

The SOM/HSFA segmentation results are strong: on five BOP datasets, SOM achieves mean AP 67.7 with a single reference view and language conditioning, competitive with supervised ZebraPoseSAT-EffNetB4 (67.5) and substantially better than annotation-free baselines such as CNOS.

Pose estimation results on LM-O and YCB-V show that STORM narrows the gap to the ground-truth-mask oracle, e.g., LM-O ADD-AUC 74.0 vs. 78.0 for FP+GT and YCB-V ADD-AUC 77.0 vs. 78.0, while outperforming the FP+CNOS baseline.

The TOM tracking verifier is a practical contribution: a BCE-trained compatibility classifier whose logit is converted into an energy-like score, smoothed temporally, and used to trigger re-localization. The stress test shows large gains over a no-recovery FoundationPose tracker (ADD-AUC 74.64 vs. 52.76) with modest overhead.

The paper includes useful ablations on HSFA depth, language conditioning, reference count, DINOv3 fine-tuning, and TOM attention, and reports runtime profiles separating one-time initialization/recovery costs from steady-state tracking costs.

The limitations section is honest and clearly states that the setting is annotation-free/adaptation-free rather than category-disjoint novel-object generalization, which is an important qualification.
The method is well motivated for robotics and physical AI, where reliable tracking under occlusion, fast motion, and viewpoint change is a real bottleneck.
Implementation details are provided in the appendix, including training hyperparameters, loss weights, data augmentation, threshold calibration, and stress-test construction.
weaknesses: Presentation quality is weak: many citations have mismatched years (e.g., Cremers & Kolev 2025 vs. 2010; LeCun et al. 2024 vs. 2006; Siméoni et al. 2022 vs. 2025; Wu et al. 2024 vs. 2025), there is a stray 'Conflict of Interest Disclosure. Let us now discuss the literature related to STORM.' in the introduction, and several table labels are confusing.

Tracking evaluation is limited: the main comparison is against FoundationPose tracking without any failure detection or recovery. There is no comparison to alternative failure detectors or trackers on standard tracking sequences, so the end-to-end benefit of TOM specifically is not fully isolated.

TOM is trained and evaluated on a synthetic failure dataset built from BOP annotations, with negatives from identity swapping and random crops. It is unclear whether TOM reliably detects gradual pose drift where the object crop remains roughly correct, which is a central real-world tracking failure mode.

The TOM attention benefit is modest in threshold-independent AUROC (95.6 to 96.4), while the large accuracy improvement (95.23% to 98.36%) may be threshold-dependent. No statistical significance tests are reported for these comparisons.

The 'energy-like' framing reduces to using the negative compatibility logit as a score. The paper acknowledges this, but the framing adds little methodological novelty and may overstate the contribution.

Segmentation gains may be partly due to auxiliary training data (SA-V, RUAPC) and the stronger frozen DINOv3 backbone, but no ablation isolates the effect of extra training data from the HSFA architecture.

The HSFA architecture is described as 'hierarchical,' but in practice it appears to be repeated self-attention/cross-attention with language conditioning. The novelty relative to standard attention is not fully established beyond HSFA0 vs. HSFA3/7 ablations.

There is a metric inconsistency: Table 8 reports AP of 94.6/95.4 for HSFA3/7, while Table 2 reports mean AP 67.7 for SOM. The metric or dataset difference is not explained, raising concerns about the comparability of the ablation.
Reproducibility is limited: no code release is mentioned, and several foundation model versions (DINOv3, SAM3D, CLIP, VLM, FoundationPose) are unspecified, making exact replication difficult.

In Table 1, the claim that 'only the mask source differs' may not hold if STORM uses SAM3D meshes while the CNOS baseline uses CAD models, making object-model quality a potential confound. The paper also does not compare the full pose pipeline to other annotation-free pose methods such as SAM6D or Pos3R.

Some claims are overstated: YCB-V 'matches the ground-truth setup exactly' is not exact (77 vs. 78 ADD, 98 vs. 99 ADD-S, 73 vs. 74 AR), and the BOP segmentation SOTA claim is marginal and within variance (67.7 vs. 67.5 mean AP).
